summary:
Players choose a destination (the Moon, Venus, or Mars), then select a rocket and an equipment package. The game updates the total cost and remaining budget with each choice. Venus and Mars require an advanced rocket. Either rocket works for the Moon. At launch, the game checks the budget and rocket compatibility. If the mission fails, the game explains why and lets players revise their choices and try again. All in-game costs are fictional and used for educational purposes.

Our team designed the player experience, including the space theme, live budget display, and launch feedback. We used Claude to help generate the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript that turn our design into a playable game, including the code that updates the budget and checks the mission rules.
details:
Space Mission Design Game is a browser-based game for high school and early college students. Players choose the Moon, Venus, or Mars, then select a rocket and an equipment package within a fictional $100 million budget. The game updates the total cost and remaining budget with each choice. At launch, it checks whether the mission is within budget and whether the rocket is compatible with the destination. If the mission fails, the game explains why so players can revise their choices and try again.

Our creative approach was to turn mission planning into a set of decisions students can experiment with. For example, a Mars mission with an advanced rocket and full equipment costs $110 million. Switching to basic equipment brings the total to $100 million while keeping the rocket required for Mars. This gives students a practical way to see how changing one resource can make a mission feasible. Robotic rovers have explored the surface of Mars (NASA, n.d.). This gives students real-world context for the game’s fictional Mars mission.

Our team considered budget limits, rocket compatibility, and how to give beginners clear feedback. We chose a space-themed interface and designed the game for a short class or science fair activity that runs on a phone or computer without an account. We used Claude to help generate the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the interface, budget calculations, and launch checks, and hosted the game on Netlify.

Our goal is to help students use feedback to improve a mission plan.
